The central question is whether the choice of positional encoding scheme — RoPE, ALiBi, learned absolute, etc. — changes which KV cache entries are safe to evict without degrading output quality during long-context inference when memory is tight. A naïve eviction policy like "drop the oldest tokens" or "drop lowest attention score" implicitly assumes that positional information is either recoverable or irrelevant after eviction, but this assumption breaks differently depending on the encoding. With RoPE, position is baked into the key and value vectors at write time via rotation, so if you evict position 1,847 and later need to attend back near it, the surviving neighbors carry rotated embeddings that were calibrated to their positions — the gap you've created isn't just a missing entry, it's a discontinuity in the positional manifold that the attention mechanism never trained to handle. With ALiBi, position is injected as a bias at attention-score time rather than into the cache vectors themselves, which means eviction changes the effective distance distribution seen during the forward pass in a way that differs structurally from the RoPE case, and what a beginner misses is that these aren't just implementation details — they determine whether an eviction policy that works well in one architecture is silently catastrophic in another.

When you evict tokens at positions, say, 512–767 and re-index survivors so position 768 becomes 512, you've changed the rotation angle applied to every key and query that references those surviving tokens — but the cached key vectors still encode the old angles from the original write time. The attention score between a new query at re-indexed position 600 and a cached key originally written at position 1,024 (now re-labeled 768) is computed using mismatched rotations: the query uses the new angle, the key carries the old one, and the dot product produces a value that corresponds to no meaningful relative distance — it's not the score for distance 168 or distance 424, it's numerical garbage with no geometric interpretation in the RoPE embedding space. Re-indexing is therefore not a neutral bookkeeping operation; it's a silent corruption. The principled fix that avoids full cache recomputation is to preserve original absolute positions and never re-index — this is what StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) effectively does by keeping the "sink" tokens and the recent window with their original position IDs intact, accepting the resulting non-contiguous position sequence rather than rewriting it. A more aggressive approach appears in work on position interpolation (Chen et al., 2023, extending LLaMA context via RoPE scaling), which suggests that smoothly scaling the position indices rather than collapsing gaps is less destructive because the model has some tolerance for compressed but monotone position sequences. What systems like H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) quietly sidestep this problem by evicting only from the recent window and never creating mid-sequence gaps — a policy choice that is architecturally motivated, not just empirically convenient, and which most benchmark comparisons fail to control for.

The attention sink phenomenon directly undermines attention score as an eviction signal because it reveals that high attention weight is partly an artifact of the softmax's need to put probability mass somewhere — not a reliable indicator of semantic importance. If a token's retention in the cache is justified by the score it receives, and those scores are distorted by sink dynamics, then the eviction ranker is working from a corrupted signal from the very first layer. H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) uses accumulated attention scores across heads and layers to decide which KV pairs to keep, and its authors show it outperforms recency-based eviction — but this comparison is made against an even weaker baseline, and the sink distortion means H2O's scores conflate "this token was genuinely attended to" with "this token absorbed sink-overflow mass from the softmax." Scissorhands (Liu et al., 2023) pushes further and shows that attention patterns are temporally persistent — tokens that were important early tend to stay important — which partially rehabilitates attention as a signal, but only if you track historical accumulation carefully and discount the first few tokens' scores explicitly, something most implementations don't do. The deeper implication, noted carefully in the PyramidKV and SnapKV work (2024), is that eviction policy validity is layer-dependent: lower layers show stronger sink concentration and weaker semantic differentiation, so a single global score threshold applied uniformly across all layers will systematically over-retain semantically vacuous tokens in early layers while potentially evicting genuinely load-bearing tokens in middle layers where attention is more semantically structured.

Uniform KV cache budget allocation across layers is, in retrospect, an operationally convenient fiction — it treats all layers as interchangeable memory consumers when empirical attention entropy distributions show they are not. PyramidKV (Cai et al., 2024) makes this concrete: they measure per-layer attention entropy across multiple architectures and find a consistent pyramid pattern where lower layers have lower entropy (more concentrated, sink-dominated attention over fewer positions) and middle-to-upper layers have higher entropy (attention spread more broadly, implying more tokens are load-bearing). The implication is that a uniform budget systematically wastes cache slots in early layers — where a small retained set would suffice — while starving middle layers where the semantic content that actually drives next-token prediction is being computed. PyramidKV's fix is to allocate cache size as an increasing function of layer depth, and they report maintaining performance at 10–20% of the full KV cache size on tasks like LongBench where uniform-budget methods at the same compression ratio degrade noticeably. SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) approaches this from a different angle — pooling attention patterns from the prompt's observation window to predict which positions will matter during generation — and implicitly arrives at a similar conclusion: the budget question cannot be separated from when in the forward pass you make the eviction decision, since early-layer scores are poor predictors of middle-layer relevance. What both papers leave underspecified is how to set the per-layer budget dynamically under hard memory pressure, since their allocations are determined offline from profiling runs rather than adapted at inference time to the actual sequence being processed.

When the input distribution shifts to code or JSON, the attention entropy profile changes structurally: code exhibits strong local syntax dependencies (brackets, indentation blocks) alongside long-range semantic jumps (function call sites to definitions), producing a bimodal entropy pattern that offline natural-language profiling will systematically mischaracterize. Concretely, a PyramidKV budget calibrated on prose will under-allocate cache to the specific middle layers that, for code, are tracking cross-function dependencies — the very tokens a static pyramid shape preserves least. The principled response is online entropy estimation: measure the actual per-layer attention entropy on the current sequence's prefill pass and use that to set the budget before generation begins, which is computationally cheap since prefill is already a full forward pass. InfLLM and later retrieval-augmented cache systems gesture at this by treating the KV cache as a dynamic store with runtime eviction decisions, but they don't explicitly recompute layer-wise budget splits per input — they adjust what to evict, not how much each layer gets. A cleaner framing comes from viewing per-layer budget allocation as a resource scheduling problem under uncertainty, where the prefill entropy profile is your signal and the allocation is a lightweight optimization (e.g., allocating proportional to normalized entropy) that runs once per request at negligible overhead relative to the prefill cost itself. The practical barrier is that most serving systems like vLLM and SGLang implement KV cache management at the block level across all layers simultaneously, so per-layer dynamic allocation requires non-trivial changes to the memory manager that the current paged-attention architecture wasn't designed to support.

Prefill entropy is a viable early-warning signal because catastrophic eviction failure has a detectable fingerprint: abnormally low entropy variance across layers (indicating sink-dominated, semantically flat attention that will mis-score every candidate for eviction) or abnormally high peak entropy in layers where the static budget is thinnest (indicating the model is spreading attention broadly precisely where you've allocated fewest cache slots). A practical detector would compute, during prefill, a per-layer entropy vector and compare it against a reference distribution derived from the calibration corpus — a simple KL divergence or z-score against empirical percentiles would flag inputs whose entropy profile falls outside the regime where the static policy was validated. In a production stack like vLLM, this fits naturally as a pre-generation hook: after the prefill forward pass but before the autoregressive loop begins, a lightweight classifier or threshold check on the entropy vector either approves the current eviction config or triggers a fallback — either switching to a more conservative policy (larger cache, recency-only eviction) or rejecting the request for rerouting to a higher-memory instance. The cost is minimal: the prefill pass already computes all attention weights, so entropy is a reduction over values you've already materialized, adding microseconds not milliseconds to request latency. What makes this non-trivial in practice is that vLLM's scheduler makes memory commitment decisions before prefill completes — it reserves KV cache blocks at request admission time — so a post-prefill policy switch requires either over-provisioning at admission or implementing speculative block reservation with a reallocation path, neither of which current block managers support cleanly. The honest engineering answer is that this early-warning system is architecturally feasible but requires decoupling request admission from cache block commitment, a refactor that touches the core of how continuous batching systems manage memory across concurrent requests.

Framing request routing as a matching problem between input entropy profiles and instance cache configurations is sound, but the information-theoretic bottleneck is immediate: you cannot know the per-layer entropy profile without running prefill, so routing decisions must be made on proxy signals extracted from the raw input before any forward pass. The proxies available pre-prefill are shallow but non-trivial — token vocabulary distribution, structural markers (bracket density, whitespace patterns, identifier-to-keyword ratios for code), sequence length, and prompt template identity — and these correlate meaningfully with entropy profile classes even if they don't determine them precisely. This is essentially a covariate-shift detection problem, and there's relevant machinery from the distribution shift literature: Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between the token distribution of an incoming request and the calibration distribution of each serving instance's current policy can be computed in O(n) over the token sequence without any model forward pass, giving a cheap routing score. The information-theoretic limit is that proxy-based routing has irreducible error whenever two inputs share the same surface statistics but produce structurally different attention patterns — a natural-language passage and a template-heavy JSON blob can have similar vocabulary entropy while triggering completely different per-layer attention distributions, and no pre-prefill signal resolves this ambiguity. Systems like Splitwise (Patel et al., 2023) and the prefill-decode disaggregation work from Microsoft already route prefill and decode to separate instance pools, which creates a natural hook: the prefill instance computes entropy, tags the request with a policy-compatibility score, and the decode instance selection happens after that signal is available, sidestepping the pre-prefill blindness entirely. The residual limit is then not informational but economic — disaggregated prefill adds network transfer latency for KV cache migration between instances, and whether policy-matched routing justifies that overhead depends on how frequently catastrophic mismatches occur in the actual request distribution, a number that currently has no published benchmark.

response:
Yes, and the bug class is distinct in a precise sense: memory-pressure eviction bugs are sins of omission (missing entries that should have been retained), whereas parallelism-mismatch transfer bugs are sins of commission (present entries that are actively wrong due to incompatible computational assumptions). The specific failure mode arises from tensor parallelism: in a TP=4 configuration, each device holds a shard of the key and value projection matrices, and the KV cache entries on each device are the outputs of that shard's projection — they are not self-contained position-encoded vectors but partial projections that only produce correct attention scores when combined across devices in the same TP group. If you transfer a KV cache from a TP=4 prefill instance to a TP=2 decode instance, the shard boundaries don't align, and naively reassembling the cache produces key vectors that mix partial projections from incompatible head partitionings — the result is not just degraded output but silently incorrect attention over the entire transferred context. RoPE compounds this because the rotation is applied after the linear projection in most implementations (following the Su et al. formulation), meaning the rotated angles are baked into the sharded projections in a way that is not easily re-sharded without recomputing the rotation — there is no cheap linear transformation that maps a TP=4 RoPE-encoded shard layout to a TP=2 one. The Mooncake system (Qin et al., 2024), which explicitly targets disaggregated KV cache transfer for inference, sidesteps this by enforcing that prefill and decode instances share identical TP configurations — a correctness constraint that significantly reduces scheduling flexibility and partially defeats the load-balancing motivation for disaggregation in the first place. The deeper architectural lesson is that KV cache entries are not portable data objects but configuration-dependent computational artifacts, and any system that treats them as freely transferable across heterogeneous instance pools is implicitly assuming a homogeneity that production clusters — with their mix of instance types and dynamic scaling — routinely violate.
